entries.topicDescription: Implicit interface satisfaction and polymorphism in Go.

tips.title: Interfaces are satisfied implicitly — no 'implements' keyword
tips.content:
In Go, a type satisfies an interface simply by implementing
all its methods. There's no explicit declaration like Java's
'implements' or Swift's conformance syntax.

This is called structural typing. If your struct has a
Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) method, it automatically
satisfies io.Reader. No import needed, no annotation.

This design enables incredible decoupling. You can define an
interface in package A that types in package B satisfy, even
if B was written years before A existed.

Keep interfaces small — one or two methods. The standard
library's io.Reader, io.Writer, and fmt.Stringer are great
examples. Small interfaces are satisfied by many types.

tips.title: Accept interfaces, return structs
tips.content:
A widely followed Go proverb: functions should accept
interfaces and return concrete types. This maximizes
flexibility for callers while keeping return types precise.

When your function accepts an interface, any type satisfying
it can be passed in. This makes your function reusable and
testable — pass a mock in tests, a real implementation in
production.

Return concrete types so callers know exactly what they get.
They can use it directly or assign it to an interface
variable if they want abstraction.

Don't define interfaces preemptively. Wait until you need
one (usually for testing or polymorphism), then define the
minimal interface at the consumer's side.

tips.title: The empty interface and type assertions
tips.content:
The empty interface (interface{} or 'any' since Go 1.18)
is satisfied by every type. It's Go's way of saying "any
value at all" — like Object in Java or Any in Kotlin.

Use type assertions to extract the concrete type from an
interface value. The two-value form (value, ok) is safe:
ok is false if the assertion fails.

Type switches let you branch on the concrete type. This is
cleaner than chaining type assertions and handles multiple
types elegantly.

Avoid overusing empty interfaces. They bypass Go's type
safety. With generics (Go 1.18+), many uses of interface{}
can be replaced with type parameters for compile-time checks.
